nameStory: Bird's-foot gets its charming name from the shape of its seed pods, which split into several narrow segments that spread out like the delicate toes of a small bird's foot. The scientific name 'perpusillus' means 'very small,' hinting at this plant's tiny, easy-to-overlook stature.
description: Bird's-foot is a diminutive annual plant in the legume family that rarely grows taller than your thumb. This low-growing herb produces tiny clusters of small white or pale yellow flowers and distinctive segmented seed pods. It's an introduced species from Europe that has established itself in a few scattered locations across New England, though it remains quite uncommon in our region.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The distinctive seed pods split into 3-5 narrow, curved segments that spread outward like bird toes - this is the plant's signature feature and easiest way to identify it

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale yellow pea-like flowers, barely 1/8 inch across, arranged in small clusters of 2-4 blooms

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small compound leaves with 5-13 oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem, soft to the touch and light green

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or cushions close to the ground, with trailing stems that feel soft and slightly fuzzy when touched

habitat: Look for bird's-foot in sandy, well-drained soils in open areas like disturbed ground, roadsides, and waste places. It prefers sunny locations with poor, acidic soils and is most likely to be found in coastal areas or sandy inland sites. This plant thrives in areas where other vegetation is sparse.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin forming their characteristic low mats of compound leaves in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Blooming occurs from late spring through summer, with the tiny white flowers quickly giving way to the diagnostic bird's-foot seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed pods are most visible in late summer and fall, when they split open and display their distinctive bird-toe shape.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds to survive until the following growing season.

funFact: Bird's-foot is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in our region's botanical surveys, making it one of the most elusive members of the legume family you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: The segmented, bird-toe-shaped seed pods are so distinctive that mature plants are unlikely to be confused with anything else. Young plants without pods might be mistaken for other small legumes, but the trailing growth habit and tiny leaflets help distinguish it.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bird's-foot,' this plant is completely unrelated to bird's-foot trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), which is a much more common yellow-flowered legume in New England. The shared common name reflects only the similar appearance of their seed pods.
compareHints: Bird's-foot is the only member of its genus (Ornithopus) found in New England. Among other small legumes in our region, it's distinguished by its extremely small size, trailing habit, and especially by those unmistakable segmented seed pods that really do look like tiny bird feet. Most other legumes produce simple pod shapes rather than these divided segments.
